Valid Palindrome.tests: Whether you can verify a mirror property in one inward walk instead of building a reversed copy, while deciding what counts as a comparable character.

3Sum.tests: Whether you can reduce a triple search to a repeated pair search by imposing order first, and keep duplicate triples out without a post-hoc dedup pass.

Remove nth Node from End of List.tests: Whether you can turn a distance from the end into a position you already hold, by launching a second pointer ahead and getting the offset right by one.

Sort Colors.tests: Holding three regions invariant in one pass, and knowing which pointer must not advance after a swap because the value it just received has never been examined.

Reverse Words in a String.tests: Whether you can reorder blocks without a temporary buffer by reversing at two scales, while normalizing the messy spacing that decides where a word actually begins.

Valid Word Abbreviation.tests: Whether you can validate a compressed encoding by walking both strings forward at once, parsing multi-digit skips and rejecting the malformed ones instead of expanding anything.

Valid Palindrome II.tests: Recognizing that a single allowed deletion turns one mismatch into exactly two candidate continuations, both of which must be tried rather than chosen greedily.

Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree.tests: Recognizing a tree question in parent-pointer disguise as the meeting of two upward chains, where sending each walker onto the other's path equalizes the distances.

Strobogrammatic Number.tests: Whether you can generalize a mirror check from equality to an arbitrary pairing rule, so the two ends must map through a table rather than simply match.

Minimum Number of Moves to Make Palindro.tests: Whether you can argue that pairing each outer character with its nearest partner from the far end is safe, and count the adjacent swaps that pairing costs.

Next Palindrome Using Same Digits.tests: Recognizing that a palindrome is fully determined by its first half, so the next larger one is the next arrangement of that half and nothing else.

Count Subarrays With Fixed Bounds.tests: Whether you can count qualifying subarrays from the last-seen positions of a few landmark values, instead of re-examining the minimum and maximum of every candidate range.

Find the Lexicographically Largest Strin.tests: Whether you can locate the best starting position among all candidate substrings in linear time by racing two candidates against each other, rather than scoring every start.

Get the Maximum Score.tests: Recognizing that two sorted paths only interact at their shared values, so the answer is the sum of the better segment between consecutive crossing points.

Create Maximum Number.tests: Whether you can split one intractable joint choice into two independent best-subsequence problems plus a small enumeration over how the length is divided between them.

Append Characters to String to Make Subs.tests: Recognizing that the answer is just where a greedy subsequence match stops, so the whole question reduces to one forward walk you already know how to run.

Squares of a Sorted Array.tests: Recognizing that with negatives present the largest magnitudes sit at the two ends, so the sorted output can be filled from the outside in.

Reverse String.tests: Whether you can run an in-place swap walk from both ends, the primitive that every later block-reversal trick is assembled from.

Intersection of Two Linked Lists.tests: Recognizing that two chains of unequal length can be equalized by letting each walker finish the other's path, so they arrive at the junction together.

Partition Labels.tests: Recognizing that each letter's last occurrence forces a minimum extent, so a part can close only once the scan has passed every commitment it made.

Remove Element.tests: Whether you can keep a write boundary that separates finished output from unscanned input, the compaction idea in its plainest form.

String Compression.tests: Whether you can write a variable-length encoding back over the input you are still reading, which only stays safe because the writer can never outrun the reader.

Rotate Array.tests: Whether you can see a rotation as a composition of reversals, and handle a shift that exceeds the array length before any of it is meaningful.

Next Permutation.tests: Whether you can find the single position where an arrangement can still grow, and see why everything to its right must then be made as small as possible.

Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array.tests: Whether you can decide keep-or-skip from a single comparison against the last kept element, and report the answer as a boundary rather than a new array.

Reverse Vowels of a String.tests: Whether you can drive a converging swap walk with a filter, advancing each pointer past everything irrelevant so only the qualifying positions ever meet.

Is Subsequence.tests: Whether you can settle a containment question with one forward walk and no extra state, plus what has to change when the same check is repeated for many queries.

Merge Strings Alternately.tests: Whether you can interleave two sequences with independent indices and finish cleanly when one runs out before the other, without special-casing the tail twice.

Compare Version Numbers.tests: Whether you can compare two sequences whose segments are neither aligned nor equal in count, treating a missing segment as zero instead of padding the strings.

Move Zeroes.tests: Whether you can compact in place while still accounting for what the vacated positions must become, in one pass rather than a copy-then-fill pair.

Longest Subarray of 1's After Deleting O.tests: Recognizing a deletion budget as a window constraint, and remembering that one element must still be removed even when the array contains no zero at all.

Backspace String Compare.tests: Whether you can compare two strings under a delete-previous rule without materializing either result, which forces the walk to run in the direction the deletions point.

Next Greater Element III.tests: Recognizing a number as a sequence of digits so a known rearrangement rule applies, with the extra obligation of rejecting results that overflow the allowed range.

Rotating the Box.tests: Whether you can separate a physical simulation into two independent steps, settling each row against its obstacles and then re-indexing, rather than reasoning about gravity post-rotation.

Happy Number.tests: Recognizing that a digit transformation is just a successor function, so asking whether the process loops forever is asking whether that chain contains a cycle.

Linked List Cycle.tests: Whether you can prove a loop exists without recording where you have been, by relying on a faster runner necessarily lapping a slower one inside any cycle.

Middle of the Linked List.tests: Whether you can locate a midpoint in one pass over a structure whose length is unknown, and decide which node counts as the middle when the count is even.

Circular Array Loop.tests: Whether you can run cycle detection where a cycle only counts if every step keeps one direction and the loop is longer than a single self-referencing element.

Find The Duplicate Number.tests: Recognizing an array as a mapping where each index points to another, so the repeated value is exactly the entrance of a cycle in that mapping.

Palindrome Linked List.tests: Whether you can restore two-directional comparison on a forward-only structure, and whether you notice the cost of the shortcut that copies every value into an array.

Linked List Cycle III.tests: Extending cycle detection past a yes-or-no answer, so the meeting point of the two runners becomes the starting evidence for a further fact about the loop.

Linked List Cycle IV.tests: Whether the constant-space cycle machinery still carries you once the question asks you to act on the loop, not merely to confirm that one exists.

Maximum Twin Sum of a Linked List.tests: Recognizing that mirrored index pairs become adjacent once the list is halved, turning a random-access pairing into two forward walks over opposite halves.

Split a Circular Linked List.tests: Whether you can find a midpoint when there is no null to stop at, and close both halves back into rings without losing either seam along the way.

Repeated DNA Sequences.tests: Recognizing that a fixed-length substring can be carried as a cheap rolling summary rather than re-extracted, so duplicate detection costs one pass and one set.

Sliding Window Maximum.tests: Whether you notice that a maximum cannot be un-added when an element leaves, and what structure has to replace the running summary once it stops being reversible.

Minimum Window Subsequence.tests: Whether you can tell a covering problem where order matters from one where it does not, since counting characters silently accepts windows that scramble the required sequence.

Longest Repeating Character Replacement.tests: Whether you can express a replacement budget as window length minus the count of the dominant character, and whether that count may safely be allowed to go stale.

Minimum Window Substring.tests: Whether you can grow until a covering requirement is met and then shrink while it still holds, tracking satisfaction with one counter instead of rechecking every character.

Longest Substring without Repeating Char.tests: Whether you can hold a no-duplicates invariant by moving only the left edge when it breaks, and see why neither edge ever needs to move backwards.

Minimum Size Subarray Sum.tests: Whether you can find a shortest qualifying window without nested loops, once you see that removing elements is the only thing that can break an already satisfied sum.

Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock.tests: Whether you can replace a search over every pair with one forward pass that carries the best option seen so far and scores each element against it.

Fruit Into Baskets.tests: Recognizing a story about baskets as the standard at-most-k-distinct window, where the hardest part is translating the rules into a constraint you can shrink against.

Frequency of the Most Frequent Element.tests: Recognizing that a budget of increments becomes a window constraint once the array is sorted, since raising everything to the window's largest value has a computable cost.

Maximum Average Subarray I.tests: Whether you can maintain a window summary by adding what enters and subtracting what leaves, instead of recomputing the whole window at every position.

Diet Plan Performance.tests: Whether you can apply a fixed-window running sum when each window produces a verdict rather than a value, accumulating a score across all windows in one pass.

Subarrays with K Different Integers.tests: Whether you can see that an exact-count condition is not shrinkable, and must be rebuilt from two monotone at-most questions that a window can actually answer.

Count Subarrays With Score Less Than K.tests: Recognizing that the score only grows as the window grows, which is what licenses the per-right-endpoint count that would be unsound for a non-monotone measure.

Count Substrings With K-Frequency Charac.tests: Whether you can count an at-least condition from the leftmost position that turns valid, and keep that scan linear when the input size removes every bit of slack.

Substring with Concatenation of All Word.tests: Whether you can slide a window whose unit is a whole word rather than a character, which means running the scan once per starting offset inside a word length.

Binary Subarrays With Sum.tests: Recognizing that an exact-sum count can be reached two ways, by differencing two at-most windows or by tallying prefix sums, and why one window alone is not enough.

Permutation in String.tests: Recognizing that containing a permutation is only a multiset claim over a window of known length, so the order inside the window never has to be examined.

Number of Substrings Containing All Thre.tests: Recognizing that once a window covering all three exists, every earlier start also works, so each right endpoint contributes a whole run of valid substrings.

Find the Index of the First Occurrence i.tests: Whether you can align a fixed-length pattern at every legal start without walking off the end, and what a failed comparison already tells you about the next start.

Max Consecutive Ones III.tests: Whether you can treat a flip budget as the window's only constraint, so the left edge advances exactly when the budget is overspent and never further.

Longest Subarray With Diff At Most Limit.tests: Whether you can keep both extremes of a growing and shrinking window available in constant time, since a plain running value cannot be undone when an element leaves.

Subarray Product Less Than K.tests: Whether you can count subarrays by summing each valid window's length instead of enumerating them, and handle the case where not even a single element qualifies.

Merge Intervals.tests: Whether you can see that ordering intervals by start turns overlap into a purely local question between what you already hold and what arrives next.

Insert Interval.tests: Holding a sorted interval list's structure intact while one new interval forces you to decide, per neighbour, whether it passes, merges, or waits.

Interval List Intersections.tests: Whether you can advance two already-sorted interval lists in step, reading overlap off the pair you hold and knowing which side is safe to discard.

Employee Free Time.tests: Recognizing that many separate schedules become one problem once you stop caring who owns each interval, and that the answer lives in what the union leaves out.

Task Scheduler.tests: Recognizing that a scheduling simulation collapses into arithmetic once you see the busiest task dictates the shape of the timeline and everything else fills its gaps.

Meeting Rooms II.tests: Whether you can stop tracking which meeting uses which room and instead measure how many are alive at the same moment as time advances.

Remove Covered Intervals.tests: Whether you can choose a sort order that makes containment decidable from one number, since ties on the start point flip which interval swallows the other.

Count Days Without Meetings.tests: Converting a coverage question into its complement, then surviving the inclusive-day arithmetic at both ends of the calendar where off-by-one errors like to hide.

Car Pooling.tests: Recognizing that capacity questions care only about the net change at each stop, so passengers become events on a timeline rather than trips to track individually.

Data Stream as Disjoint Intervals.tests: Designing a structure that keeps a set of intervals disjoint under arbitrary single-point insertions, where one new value can bridge two separate blocks into one.

Minimum Interval to Include Each Query.tests: Whether you can reorder independent queries so a single ordered pass over the intervals serves them all, instead of re-searching the whole list per query.

Reverse Linked List.tests: Whether you can flip a chain's direction one link at a time without losing hold of the node you are about to orphan.

Reverse Nodes in k-Group.tests: Whether your pointer bookkeeping survives repeated bounded reversals, including the rule that a trailing partial group must be left exactly as it was found.

Reverse Linked List II.tests: Whether you can confine a reversal to a window and still reattach both seams correctly, given that the window's head becomes its tail.

Reorder List.tests: Recognizing a weave of front and back as three familiar list routines composed in order, rather than one clever traversal you have never met.

Swapping Nodes in a Linked List.tests: Whether you can locate two positions measured from opposite ends in a single traversal, staying clear about which end each index counts from.

Reverse Nodes In Even Length Groups.tests: Whether you can drive a reversal routine from a group size that grows as you walk, while a truncated final group changes whether it qualifies.

Swap Nodes in Pairs.tests: Whether you can rewire adjacent nodes without touching their values, and handle the head itself being one of the nodes that moves.

Split Linked List in Parts.tests: Whether you can compute every part's size before cutting anything, then sever once at each boundary under the rule that earlier parts absorb the remainder.

Remove Linked List Elements.tests: Whether you can delete by redirecting a predecessor's pointer rather than touching the node itself, including when the node to drop is the head.

Delete N Nodes After M Nodes of a Linked.tests: Keeping two counters honest across a repeating keep-then-drop cycle, so the traversal terminates cleanly when the list runs out in the middle of a cycle.

Remove Duplicates from Sorted List.tests: Whether you exploit sortedness so equality only ever needs checking against the immediate neighbour, and a whole run of copies collapses without restarting the scan.

Insert into a Sorted Circular Linked Lis.tests: Whether you can find an insertion seam in a cycle that has no end, including the cases where every value is equal or the list is empty.

Odd Even Linked List.tests: Whether you can grow two separate chains during one pass and join them at the end, instead of moving nodes individually into their final positions.

Rotate List.tests: Recognizing that rotation is really a choice of where to cut, and that the shift count must first be reduced against the list's own length.

Maximize Capital.tests: Whether you can separate what you can currently afford from what you cannot, and let each new gain move items across that line before you choose again.

Find Median from a Data Stream.tests: Designing storage where the middle of a growing collection is always immediately readable, rather than something you recompute after every insertion.

Sliding Window Median.tests: Whether a balanced two-sided structure survives elements leaving as well as arriving, when the container you would reach for cannot remove from its interior.

Schedule Tasks on Minimum Machines.tests: Recognizing that a machine count question is really about peak simultaneous demand, so the earliest finishing task decides whether a new machine is needed.

Meeting Rooms III.tests: Whether you can track free and busy rooms at once with correct tie-breaking, since a delayed meeting must take the lowest-numbered room among those freeing first.

Minimum Cost to Connect Sticks.tests: Whether you trust that combining the two cheapest pieces first is safe, and that each merged result re-enters the pool as an ordinary candidate.

Longest Happy String.tests: Whether a greedy that spends the most plentiful letter can be constrained by recent history, falling back when the obvious choice would break the run rule.

Maximum Average Pass Ratio.tests: Recognizing that the right greedy key is how much a single addition improves a class, not how badly the class is currently performing.

The Number of the Smallest Unoccupied Ch.tests: Whether you can process arrivals and departures in the correct order while keeping freed resources reusable by lowest index rather than most recently released.

Largest Number After Digit Swaps by Pari.tests: Recognizing that a swap restriction partitions digits into independent pools, so each position can only ever be improved from within its own pool.

Find Right Interval.tests: Recognizing a nearest-thing-that-starts-after-this-ends question as a successor lookup, which needs a searchable order built without losing the original indices.

Construct Target Array with Multiple Sum.tests: Recognizing that a forward construction is hopelessly ambiguous but the final step never is, so the process is only decidable when replayed from the finished array.

Merge Sorted Array.tests: Whether you can merge in place by choosing a fill direction in which writing never overwrites data you have not read yet.

Kth Smallest Number in M Sorted Lists.tests: Whether you can hold just one live candidate per sorted source, so the next-smallest element overall is always available without scanning the rest.

Find K Pairs with Smallest Sums.tests: Recognizing that pairs you never actually build still form sorted sequences, so a small frontier of candidates always contains the next-best pair.

Merge K Sorted Lists.tests: Whether you can exploit the order already present inside each input instead of discarding it, keeping the cost tied to the number of lists rather than elements.

Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix.tests: Whether you can use sortedness in two directions at once, since reading the matrix row by row throws away half the guarantee you were handed.

K-th Smallest Prime Fraction.tests: Whether you can impose a sorted structure on values built from two arrays, when the ordering you need is not the ordering the arrays came in.

Super Ugly Number.tests: Recognizing that each prime generates its own increasing sequence over answers you have already produced, and that the same value arrives from several directions.

Kth Largest Element in a Stream.tests: Designing a container that only ever needs to remember k values, discarding anything that can no longer influence the answer the moment it arrives.

Reorganize String.tests: Recognizing that only the most frequent character can make the arrangement impossible, and that every placement decision depends on counts rather than the letters themselves.

K Closest Points to Origin.tests: Whether you can beat a full sort when only k winners matter, and notice that a monotone transform of distance is enough for every comparison.

Top K Frequent Elements.tests: Whether you can move a problem off the values and onto their tallies, then apply selection machinery to counts you built in one pass.

Kth Largest Element in an Array.tests: Whether you can find a single order statistic without sorting everything, keeping only the elements that could still turn out to be the answer.

Maximal Score After Applying K Operation.tests: Whether you can let a mutated element compete again, since taking the current largest changes its value but does not remove it from consideration.

Find the Kth Largest Integer in the Arra.tests: Whether you notice numeric ordering must be reconstructed for values too large to convert, where length decides first and content only ever breaks ties.

Third Maximum Number.tests: Whether you can track a fixed number of leaders in one pass while duplicates and a missing third rank quietly change what the answer should be.

Find Subsequence of Length K with the La.tests: Whether you can select by value but emit by position, keeping the chosen survivors in their original order once the selection has been made.

Minimum Cost to Hire K Workers.tests: Recognizing that fixing one worker's pay rate makes every other cost computable, turning a two-variable optimization into a sweep with a bounded selection inside.

Smallest Range Covering Elements from K.tests: Recognizing that a range touching every list is pinned by one element per list, and that only one end of it can usefully move at a time.

Maximum Performance of a Team.tests: Recognizing that a product of two competing quantities becomes tractable once one of them is fixed as the team's limiting factor and the other is selected freely.

K Maximum Sum Combinations From Two Arra.tests: Whether you can avoid building every pair sum, expanding only the neighbours of combinations you already accepted while refusing to revisit the same one twice.

K Empty Slots.tests: Recognizing that inverting the given mapping turns an evolving picture into a static array, where the condition becomes a statement about one fixed-width span.

Find the K-Sum of an Array.tests: Whether you can reason about an exponential space of subset sums as deviations from the single best one, generating candidates in order instead of enumerating them.

Maximum Product After K Increments.tests: Recognizing that spending each unit on the currently smallest factor maximizes a product, and being able to argue why that choice is never regretted later.

Least Number of Unique Integers after K.tests: Recognizing that eliminating whole groups matters more than removing many elements, so the cheapest groups to erase completely are the ones to spend on first.

Final Array State After K Multiplication.tests: Whether you can repeatedly serve the current minimum and return the changed value to the pool, with ties resolved by earliest position rather than arbitrarily.

Binary Search.tests: Whether you can maintain a shrinking interval that provably still contains the target, and terminate cleanly, without off-by-one drift in the bounds.

Search in Rotated Sorted Array.tests: Recognizing that a local check at the midpoint still proves which half is properly ordered, so a broken sort order does not cost you the halving.

First Bad Version.tests: Whether you can see an API's yes/no answers as a monotone sequence with one flip point, and search for that boundary instead of for values.

Find K Closest Elements.tests: Recognizing that the answer is a contiguous block of the sorted array, so the search is for where that block begins rather than for k separate elements.

Single Element in a Sorted Array.tests: Recognizing that pairing adjacent positions creates a parity invariant that breaks exactly at the intruder, so index arithmetic rather than value comparison chooses the half.

Split Array Largest Sum.tests: Whether you can invert the question and search for the answer value itself, testing feasibility of a guess, when computing the optimal partition directly resists a formula.

The K Weakest Rows in a Matrix.tests: Recognizing that each row's soldier count is itself a boundary lookup, and that ranking only needs the k smallest rather than a full ordering.

Maximum Value at a Given Index in a Boun.tests: Whether you can compute the total cost of a candidate peak in closed form, handling the clamp at one and the array edges without off-by-one error.

Search in Rotated Sorted Array II.tests: Holding the rotated-array halving argument while duplicates make the midpoint uninformative, and knowing what that ambiguity costs you in the worst case.

Count Pairs Whose Sum is Less than Targe.tests: Whether you can beat the obvious double loop by sorting first, so each element's valid partners form one contiguous stretch you can count directly.

Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array II.tests: Whether you can still discard half of a rotated array when equal endpoints hide the rotation, and justify the one safe step left when you cannot.

Maximum Running Time of N Computers.tests: Recognizing that a scheduling question with swappable batteries is a feasibility test on a guessed runtime, once you see what caps a single battery's usable charge.

Minimize Max Distance to Gas Station.tests: Holding the guess-and-check structure while the candidates are real numbers, so termination comes from a precision target rather than from integer bounds collapsing.

Divide Chocolate.tests: Whether you can flip a minimize-the-maximum template into maximize-the-minimum, and keep the feasibility check honest about what a failed cut actually proves.

Split Array Into Two Arrays to Minimize.tests: Recognizing that an exponential subset search splits into two enumerable halves whose sums can be matched by sorted lookup instead of by pairing every combination.

Number of Flowers in Full Bloom.tests: Recognizing that how many things are active at a moment is a difference of two counts over sorted event times, making each query a pair of lookups.

Koko Eating Bananas.tests: Whether you can spot that the unknown is a rate whose feasibility only ever improves as it grows, which makes the rate itself the thing to search.

Search Insert Position.tests: Whether you can return the boundary where a missing element would belong, not just a found index, which is the shape most binary searches actually need.

Find Peak Element.tests: Recognizing that an uphill neighbor guarantees a peak lies in that direction, so a local slope check discards half of an array that is not sorted at all.

Find First and Last Position of Element.tests: Whether you can write the same search twice with different tie-breaking, so a run of equal values resolves to its left edge once and its right edge the other time.

Kth Smallest Product of Two Sorted Array.tests: Whether you can count values at or below a guess when negative factors reverse every inequality, so the counting oracle needs cases the positive version never had.

Sqrt(x).tests: Whether you can search a numeric range for the largest value whose square still fits, treating the answer itself rather than any array as the search space.

Reaching Points.tests: Recognizing that a forward search branching two ways at every step becomes deterministic when replayed backwards from the target, which is what makes it tractable.

Kth Missing Positive Number.tests: Whether you can express how many values are missing before each index as a monotone quantity, turning a linear walk into a boundary lookup.

Subsets.tests: Whether you can see an exponential output as a tree of per-element choices, and keep the shared working list honest by undoing each choice on the way back.

Permutations.tests: Whether you can fill positions from a shrinking pool of unused elements, tracking availability instead of a start index, now that reorderings count as distinct answers.

Letter Combinations of a Phone Number.tests: Recognizing that a fixed-length product of independent choice sets is the same recursion as subsets, with each position's candidates supplied by a lookup rather than the input.

Generate Parentheses.tests: Recognizing that a validity rule can be checked on partial output, so impossible prefixes die early instead of after a full candidate is built and tested.

Find K-Sum Subsets.tests: Whether an added numeric target turns the include-or-exclude walk from a plain enumeration into a search, where the running total decides which branches stay worth entering.

Letter Case Permutation.tests: Recognizing that only letters branch while digits are forced, turning a permutation-sounding ask into an independent two-way choice at a subset of the positions.

Letter Tile Possibilities.tests: Holding the slot-filling recursion while repeated tiles threaten identical sequences, which forces branching to key on distinct values rather than on positions.

Subsets II.tests: Whether you can prevent duplicate results at the moment of branching rather than generating them and filtering afterwards, once the input can hold repeated values.

Jump Game I.tests: Whether you can replace which path do I take with how far can I get, a reframing that turns an exponential path search into a single sweep.

Boats to Save People.tests: Whether you can argue that the hardest item to place should be settled first, and that its best partner is forced once the list is sorted.

Gas Stations.tests: Recognizing that a failed run rules out every start inside it, not just the one you tried, which is what collapses a quadratic check into one pass.

Two City Scheduling.tests: Recognizing that the decision turns on the difference between two costs rather than either cost alone, so the sort key is a quantity the input never states.

Minimum Number of Refueling Stops.tests: Recognizing that a refuel can be decided in hindsight, since a station you passed stays available, so the choice need not be made when you reach it.

Largest Palindromic Number.tests: Whether you can build half of a mirrored answer from digit counts while leading-zero and middle-digit rules quietly invalidate the obvious construction.

Jump Game II.tests: Holding the reachability frontier while now counting layers, so the move count comes from how often the frontier is exhausted rather than from any chosen route.

Number of Steps to Reduce a Binary Numbe.tests: Recognizing that a number too large to hold can still be reduced digit by digit, with one carry bit standing in for all the arithmetic.

Rearranging Fruits.tests: Recognizing that only the mismatched surplus has to move, and that the cheapest way to trade two costly items may route through a third, lighter one.

Maximum Swap.tests: Whether you can find the earliest position a single exchange can improve, and pick among equally good partners the one that leaves the rest of the number best.

Can Place Flowers.tests: Whether you can commit to each opportunity the moment it is legal, trusting that an early placement never blocks a better arrangement later.

Largest Odd Number in String.tests: Recognizing that the answer must be a prefix of the input, which reduces an apparent search over substrings to locating one character.

Assign Cookies.tests: Whether you can spend the smallest sufficient resource on each demand, and see why saving a larger one for later never loses.

Candy.tests: Whether you can satisfy a constraint that looks in both directions when a single sweep can only ever enforce one of them.

Minimum Replacements to Sort the Array.tests: Recognizing that the array must be read from the right, since each element's ceiling is fixed by what follows, and that splitting as evenly as possible minimizes the pieces.

Sort an Array.tests: Whether you can write a comparison sort end to end yourself, the recursive split, the merge or partition step and the base cases, without a library call.

Text Justification.tests: Whether you can hold a pile of interacting formatting rules, line packing, uneven space distribution and the last line's exception, without one case corrupting another.

Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II.tests: Recognizing that unlimited transactions make every upward step independently collectible, so no decision about when to hold is ever needed.

Wildcard Matching.tests: Whether you can let one wildcard absorb an unknown amount of input while keeping the work polynomial, instead of branching on every length it might take.

Remove K Digits.tests: Recognizing that a digit is worth deleting only when a smaller one follows it, and that one deletion can make an earlier digit newly worth deleting.

Largest Number.tests: Recognizing that the ordering you need is defined by the result of combining two pieces, not by comparing them as numbers, and that it must still be a valid order.

Strong Password Checker.tests: Whether you can reconcile three requirements whose cheapest repairs overlap, so counting each in isolation overstates the work and the length rules change which repair wins.

Maximum Points After Enemy Battles.tests: Recognizing that one extreme element should carry every scoring move while the rest exist only to be cashed in for the resource that funds them.

Integer to Roman.tests: Whether you can encode a value system as an ordered table, subtractive exceptions included, so one descending sweep replaces a pile of special cases.

N-Queens II.tests: Whether you can count arrangements without ever building one, keeping conflicts in occupancy sets so the answer accumulates from the search itself rather than from inspecting finished boards.

Word Search.tests: Whether you can reserve a cell for the path you are currently on and release it on the way out, so sibling branches are never wrongly blocked.

House Robber III.tests: Whether you can carry two answers up from every subtree, the best with this node taken and the best without, when there is no linear order to index.

Restore IP Addresses.tests: Whether you can bound a segmentation search by both piece count and piece legality, catching the leading-zero and range rules that a plain numeric parse quietly accepts.

Flood Fill.tests: Whether you can spread through a connected region while making each visit permanent, since a region fill must not undo its marks the way a path search does.

Minimum Moves to Spread Stones Over Grid.tests: Recognizing that surplus cells and empty cells pair up independently, so the cost is a matching problem measured in Manhattan distance rather than a sequence of simulated moves.

Sudoku Solver.tests: Whether you can keep row, column, and box occupancy updated in step with each placement, so testing a candidate costs nothing and the expense stays in the branching.

Matchsticks to Square.tests: Whether you can make an exponential assignment search finish through pruning alone: order items so failures come early, and refuse groups whose partial totals are already identical.

Binary Watch.tests: Recognizing a watch face as a fixed set of bits, so 'exactly n lit' becomes enumeration over a chosen popcount, filtered down to the readings that are legal times.

Optimal Account Balancing.tests: Recognizing that the individual transactions stop mattering once each person collapses to a net balance, turning the ask into a fewest-settlements search over a zero-sum multiset.

Split a String Into the Max Number of Un.tests: Whether you can thread the set of already-committed pieces through the recursion, because a cut's legality here depends on the history of the split, not on the segment alone.

Binary Tree Paths.tests: Whether you can grow one root-to-here trail, snapshot it at each leaf, and pop on the way back so a sibling branch never inherits a stale suffix.

All Paths From Source to Target.tests: Whether you can enumerate every route without a visited set, seeing that acyclicity is exactly what makes revisiting a node on a different path safe.

Map Sum Pairs.tests: Whether you can decide what a prefix node should store so a sum query is one walk, and handle a key being reinserted with a different value.

Check If a Word is a Prefix of Any Word.tests: Whether you can express "is a prefix of" precisely enough to compare against each token directly, without reaching for a structure this input size does not need.

Longest Word With All Prefixes.tests: Whether you enforce a condition at every node along a path instead of only at its end, so an invalid prefix prunes everything beneath it immediately.

Design HashMap.tests: Whether you can build the structure you normally get for free, choosing how keys land in buckets and what happens when two of them land together.

Fraction to Recurring Decimal.tests: Recognizing that a repeating decimal is a repeated remainder, and that knowing a repeat happened is useless unless you also remember where it first occurred.

Logger Rate Limiter.tests: Whether you store a timestamp rather than a flag per key, and decide exactly when the stored value should advance so the window measures from the right event.

Next Greater Element I.tests: Whether you answer every query from a table built in one pass over the reference array, instead of restarting the search through it for each element.

Isomorphic Strings.tests: Whether you test a structural correspondence in both directions at once, since a mapping that is consistent one way can still collapse two distinct characters the other.

Find Duplicate File in System.tests: Whether you can see past a messy input format to the one field that should be the key, and keep the parsing separate from the grouping it feeds.

Longest Palindrome.tests: Recognizing that only pair counts matter, so the length follows from summing the even portion of each letter's frequency and allowing at most one leftover center.

Continuous Subarray Sum.tests: Whether you can replace the prefix sum with a coarser state that still separates the cases, and respect a length requirement that a plain seen-map ignores.

Unique Number of Occurrences.tests: Whether you can treat the frequency table as data in its own right, asking a question about the counts rather than about the values that produced them.

High Five.tests: Whether you can bucket records by a key and keep only the small slice of each bucket that matters, instead of sorting everything you were handed.

Bulls and Cows.tests: Whether you can count two overlapping relationships without letting an exact match also be counted as a misplaced one, ideally in a single pass over both strings.

Number of Wonderful Substrings.tests: Recognizing that only each letter's parity matters, which compresses a substring property into a small state whose earlier occurrences you can tally as you sweep.

Number of Distinct Islands.tests: Whether you can turn a set of cells into a signature that ignores absolute position but preserves shape, so two identical islands hash to the same key.

Custom Sort String.tests: Whether you can express an arbitrary ordering as a lookup from character to rank, and decide where characters absent from that ordering are allowed to land.

Total Appeal of a String.tests: Whether you can stop enumerating substrings and instead total each position's own contribution, using how far back the same character last appeared.

Dot Product of Two Sparse Vectors.tests: Whether you choose a representation that stores only what exists, and make the pairing step iterate the stored entries instead of the vector's full logical length.

Longest Happy Prefix.tests: Whether you can compare a prefix against a suffix without re-reading either, by carrying a value that updates in constant time as the window extends.

Find Longest Self-Contained Substring.tests: Whether you can shrink the search to boundaries that some character's full occurrence range forces, instead of testing every substring for leakage outside it.

Intersection of Two Arrays.tests: Whether you convert membership testing into a constant-time question by loading one side into a set, and let the same structure handle deduplication for free.

Word Pattern.tests: Recognizing a bijection check under new clothing, where the two sides are different kinds of token and both directions of the mapping still have to hold.

Valid Sudoku.tests: Whether you can validate three independent constraint families in one pass, and derive a cell's block identity arithmetically instead of scanning each block separately.

Roman to Integer.tests: Whether you can encode symbol values as a lookup and handle subtraction by comparing each symbol with its neighbor, rather than enumerating every special two-letter case.

Contiguous Array.tests: Recognizing that an equal-counts condition becomes a running-balance condition once the two values are weighted against each other, turning the search into matching earlier states.

Jewels and Stones.tests: Whether you notice a nested membership scan collapses the moment one side is loaded into a set, the cheapest possible instance of trading space for lookups.

Vowel Spellchecker.tests: Whether you can layer several normalizations in strict precedence, each answering a more forgiving question, while keeping the earliest matching entry for every key.

N-Repeated Element in Size 2N Array.tests: Whether the first repeat you encounter is enough, once you notice how the guaranteed multiplicity constrains where two copies can hide relative to each other.

Powerful Integers.tests: Whether you can bound a double enumeration by the answer's own limit and notice the degenerate base that makes the loop never terminate.

Before and After Puzzle.tests: Whether you index phrases by their joinable endpoints so pairing becomes a lookup, and handle a phrase never pairing with itself while duplicate results still collapse.

Intersection of Two Arrays II.tests: Whether you can tell when multiplicity is part of the answer, and pick the counting version of the membership oracle instead of the one that silently deduplicates.

Subarray Sum Equals K.tests: Whether you can rewrite a range condition as a difference between two running totals, so counting qualifying ranges becomes one pass and a tally of earlier states.

Identify the Largest Outlier in an Array.tests: Recognizing that the defining equation fixes each candidate's partner, so the search becomes one lookup per element with counts guarding against reusing a single element twice.

Find the Length of the Longest Common Pr.tests: Whether you avoid comparing every pair by storing one side's prefixes in a set, so each candidate is tested by shrinking it until something matches.

Palindrome Permutation.tests: Whether you can decide a rearrangement question from parity alone, testing the letters' counts rather than searching the arrangements they could produce.

Valid Anagram.tests: Whether you can replace sorting with counting when order is irrelevant, and see that two strings match exactly when their small count tables do.

Design Tic-Tac-Toe.tests: Whether you can answer a win query in constant time by maintaining summary counters as moves arrive, instead of rescanning the board after each one.

Group Anagrams.tests: Whether you can derive a canonical key from each element so that grouping becomes a single hash-map bucketing pass rather than pairwise comparison.

Maximum Frequency Stack.tests: Whether you can serve a most-frequent-then-most-recent pop in constant time, which needs state organized by count rather than a single stack or a recomputed maximum.

First Unique Character in a String.tests: Whether you can pair a completed count table with a second ordered scan, since the earliest qualifying element cannot be identified while counts are still changing.

Find All Anagrams in a String.tests: Whether you can beat rebuilding a comparison from scratch at every position by updating a fixed-size summary as one element enters and one leaves.

Longest Palindrome by Concatenating Two-.tests: Recognizing that the answer depends only on how many units pair with their reverse, and that self-mirrored units obey a stricter rule than the rest.

Ransom Note.tests: Whether you can express containment as a budget check over counts, spending from a tally of available characters instead of searching the source string repeatedly.

Minimum Number of Pushes to Type Word II.tests: Recognizing a cost-assignment problem behind a keypad story, where the cheapest slots must go to the most frequent letters and only the counts matter.

Rank Teams by Votes.tests: Whether you can build a comparison key that is itself a vector of tallies, with every tiebreak level encoded explicitly rather than left to the default ordering.

Pairs of Songs With Total Durations Divi.tests: Whether you can replace the nested pair scan with a single pass that counts, for each element, the earlier partners that complete it under modular arithmetic.

Count Anagrams.tests: Whether you can count arrangements without enumerating them, and handle the division that formula demands inside modular arithmetic where dividing is not allowed.

Divide Array Into Increasing Sequences.tests: Recognizing that a partition feasibility question collapses to a single inequality about the most repeated value, so no actual partition ever needs constructing.

Max Consecutive Ones.tests: Whether you can track a current run and a best-so-far in one sweep, resetting cleanly at each break instead of re-measuring streaks from every index.

Count and Say.tests: Whether you can implement a run-length description precisely and iterate it, keeping the boundary handling correct when a run ends exactly at the string's end.

Find Words That Can Be Formed by Charact.tests: Whether you can reuse one budget table across many independent checks without letting an earlier word's consumption corrupt the counts available to the next.

Check if One String Swap Can Make String.tests: Whether you can reason exhaustively about how few positions are allowed to differ, and what must hold between them, before any comparison code is written.

Find Pivot Index.tests: Whether you can decide a left-versus-right balance at every index using one running total and a fixed grand total, rather than summing both sides repeatedly.

Sort Array by Increasing Frequency.tests: Whether you can sort by a key that lives outside the elements themselves, built from a finished count table with the tiebreak direction stated deliberately.

Concatenation of Array.tests: Whether you can construct an output array by index arithmetic in a single allocation, keeping the mapping from source position to destination position obvious.

Zigzag Conversion.tests: Whether you can translate a visual layout into a row assignment rule, tracking direction reversals at the boundaries instead of literally drawing the grid.

Zero Array Transformation I.tests: Recognizing that many overlapping range updates need only their per-index coverage, which a marker-at-the-edges sweep produces without touching each element of each range.

Count Binary Substrings.tests: Whether you can beat checking every substring by noticing the answer decomposes over adjacent runs, so only consecutive run lengths need comparing.

Redundant Connection.tests: Whether you can detect a cycle as it forms by asking, before each edge is added, whether its endpoints already belong to the same component.

Number of Islands.tests: Whether you can convert an adjacency picture into component counting, deciding deliberately between traversal and merging when the grid will not change afterward.

Most Stones Removed with Same Row or Col.tests: Recognizing a removal-count question as a component-count question, where sharing a coordinate is the only relationship that matters and the order of removals does not.

Longest Consecutive Sequence.tests: Whether you can beat the sorting solution by treating consecutive values as a grouping relation, and by knowing which elements are safe to start counting from.

Last Day Where You Can Still Cross.tests: Recognizing that union-find can absorb additions but not deletions, which forces you to choose a direction to process time in before writing any code.

Regions Cut by Slashes.tests: Recognizing that a cell cannot be a single node once a diagonal cuts through it, so the modeling decision carries this problem rather than the merging code.

Accounts Merge.tests: Whether you can group records through a shared attribute without comparing every pair, then reassemble each finished component back into the output format required.

Minimize Malware Spread.tests: Whether you can attribute a global outcome back to single nodes, which turns on how many infected nodes a component already contains and on the stated tiebreak.

Evaluate Division.tests: Recognizing chained ratios as a graph where each edge carries a multiplier, so answering a query means composing multipliers along a connection rather than solving equations.

Find if Path Exists in Graph.tests: Whether you can answer reachability without producing a path, reducing the question to whether two vertices end up in the same component after all edges are absorbed.

The Skyline Problem.tests: Whether you can turn overlapping rectangles into an ordered stream of boundary events and emit a point only when the tallest active height actually changes.

Similar String Groups.tests: Whether you can group by a relation that has no exact shared key, accepting a quadratic pairwise test when the alternative depends on which input dimension is smaller.

Optimize Water Distribution in a Village.tests: Recognizing a minimum spanning tree under a story with two kinds of cost, and finding a way to express the second kind in the same currency as the first.

Number of Islands II.tests: Whether you can maintain a region count incrementally as cells appear, when a single new cell may join several existing regions at once.

Snapshot Array.tests: Whether you can make versioning cheap by recording only what actually changed, so a snapshot costs nothing and a historical read pays a small search instead.

Time-Based Key-Value Store.tests: Whether you can exploit the fact that writes arrive in increasing time order, turning a get-as-of query into a search over already-sorted history rather than a scan.

Implement LRU Cache.tests: Whether you can hold two views of the same data in sync, so that lookup and eviction are both constant time instead of one of them degrading to a scan.

Insert Delete GetRandom O(1).tests: Whether you can keep uniform random access alive under deletion, which means deciding what an array is allowed to do when a hole opens in its middle.

Min Stack.tests: Whether you can answer a minimum query in constant time on a structure whose contents keep leaving, which rules out storing a single current minimum.

Range Module.tests: Whether you can maintain a set of intervals under both addition and removal, keeping them disjoint and merged so a containment query stays a single lookup.

Shortest Word Distance II.tests: Whether you can pay once at construction so repeated queries stay cheap, comparing two already-ordered position lists rather than rescanning the words each time.

LFU Cache.tests: Whether you can evict by frequency and break ties by recency in constant time, which needs the counts themselves to become an addressable part of the structure.

Moving Average from Data Stream.tests: Whether you can maintain an aggregate by adjusting it with each arrival and departure, so no query ever re-adds the elements currently inside the window.

Two Sum III - Data structure design.tests: Whether you can choose where a structure's cost should sit, since making insertion cheap and lookup cheap at the same time is not free here.

Range Sum Query - Immutable.tests: Whether you can recognize that immutable data invites precomputation, so every range answer becomes a difference of two stored totals rather than a fresh loop.

Design HashSet.tests: Whether you can build the primitive you normally import, choosing a bucket scheme and a collision policy and defending both against adversarial key distributions.

Max Stack.tests: Whether you can support removing the maximum, not just reading it, which breaks the simple companion-stack trick that makes reading a maximum easy.

Stream of Characters.tests: Whether you can answer suffix-matching queries on an unbounded stream, which forces a decision about which end of the stored words you index them by.

All O'one Data Structures.tests: Whether you can keep both extremes of a frequency distribution reachable in constant time while counts move by one, which no single sorted container gives you.

Finding MK Average.tests: Whether you can maintain a trimmed aggregate under a sliding window, where each arrival and eviction may shift which elements are excluded from the total.

Find the Difference.tests: Whether you can see two nearly identical letter multisets as one stream where matched items annihilate, leaving the intruder, without building a frequency table.

Complement of Base 10 Integer.tests: Whether you can build a mask that spans exactly the number's own bit width, rather than assuming a fixed 32-bit word, before inverting anything.

Flipping an Image.tests: Whether you can fuse two stated passes into one inward walk, noticing that a mirrored pair whose values already agree needs different handling from one that does not.

Single Number.tests: Whether you can find the unpaired element using an operation that is order-blind and self-cancelling, instead of counting occurrences in extra memory.

Single Number II.tests: Whether you can rebuild the cancellation idea when duplicates arrive in threes, which forces you to count evidence per bit position rather than keep one running total.

Encode and Decode Strings.tests: Designing a self-delimiting wire format so arbitrary string content, including your own separator characters, survives a round trip through a single flat string.

Reverse Bits.tests: Whether you can move bits between two numbers one position at a time while holding the width fixed, and what you would change if the function were called repeatedly.

Find the Longest Substring Having Vowels.tests: Recognizing that a parity requirement over a tiny alphabet is really a small state carried along the string, and that two positions sharing a state delimit a valid stretch.

Longest Subarray With Maximum Bitwise AN.tests: Whether you can reason about what bitwise AND can never do to a value, which collapses an apparent search over subarrays into a much simpler scan.

Count Triplets That Can Form Two Arrays.tests: Recognizing that requiring two adjacent halves to match makes the split point irrelevant, turning a triple loop into a question about equal range endpoints.

Sum of All Subset XOR Totals.tests: Whether you can replace enumerating every subset with a per-bit argument about how often a given bit can survive across all of them.

Find The K-th Lucky Number.tests: Recognizing that a language built from exactly two symbols is indexed by counting, so the kth string is read off an arithmetic value instead of generated.

Minimum Number of K Consecutive Bit Flip.tests: Holding a running count of how many earlier flips still cover the current index, so a greedy left-to-right sweep never has to touch k cells per operation.

Minimum One Bit Operations to Make Integ.tests: Whether you can find the hidden ordering the two allowed moves impose on all integers, turning an apparent search over states into a rank computation.

Triples with Bitwise AND Equal To Zero.tests: Whether you can precompute over the bounded value space instead of the input, so a cubic triple search becomes counting pairs once and reusing that table.

Power of Two.tests: Whether you can express exactly-one-bit-set as a single arithmetic identity, and remember that zero and negative inputs must not sneak through it.

Hamming Distance.tests: Whether you can turn positions-where-two-numbers-differ into one derived value whose set bits are exactly what needs counting.

Minimum Operations to Make the Integer Z.tests: Whether you can fix the operation count first and then test feasibility, using how few and how many powers of two a given value can decompose into.

Minimum Area Rectangle.tests: Whether you can pin a rectangle down by one diagonal pair and let a membership test supply the remaining corners, avoiding a search over four-point combinations.

Maximum Area Rectangle With Point Constr.tests: Whether you can enumerate candidate corner pairs and still verify the nothing-inside-or-on-the-border rule, without letting that verification quietly become the dominant cost.

Reverse Integer.tests: Whether you can detect overflow before it happens while peeling digits, since the reversed value need not fit the same type the input comfortably did.

Minimum Number of Lines to Cover Points.tests: Reading a tiny input bound as permission to search over subsets, while testing collinearity exactly rather than through slopes that break on vertical pairs.

Minimize Manhattan Distances.tests: Whether you can change coordinates so Manhattan distance becomes a per-axis extreme, making remove-the-one-worst-point a question about a handful of boundary candidates.

Convex Polygon.tests: Whether you can express convexity as every consecutive turn agreeing in direction, using an integer test that never divides and never measures an angle.

Check If It Is a Straight Line.tests: Whether you can test collinearity with a comparison that stays in exact integers, instead of a slope that blows up the moment two points share an x.

Minimum Cuts to Divide a Circle.tests: Whether you can resist drawing the cuts and reason about parity instead, noticing that one small input refuses to follow whatever formula the rest obey.

Valid Square.tests: Whether you can pick an invariant that identifies a square regardless of the order the four points arrive in, and never take a square root to check it.

Rectangle Overlap.tests: Whether you can decompose a two-dimensional overlap question into two independent one-dimensional ones, and decide deliberately whether touching edges should count.

Minimum Time Visiting All Points.tests: Recognizing that when a diagonal step costs the same as a straight one, the two axis gaps stop adding together and one of them alone dictates the cost.

Rectangle Area.tests: Whether you can compute a union by adding both areas and subtracting what they share, with the shared part measured per axis and clamped at zero.

Queries on Number of Points Inside a Cir.tests: Whether you can compare distances without square roots, keeping every containment test in exact integer arithmetic once the input bounds make direct checking acceptable.

Max Points on a Line.tests: Whether you can fix one point as an anchor and group the rest by direction, choosing a direction key that survives vertical lines and repeated points.

Maximum Number of Visible Points.tests: Whether you can sort by angle and treat a field of view as a window sliding over that order, handling the wraparound past a full turn and points underfoot.

Detonate the Maximum Bombs.tests: Recognizing a one-way reachability graph inside a geometry statement, since one bomb covering another says nothing at all about the reverse direction.

Self Crossing.tests: Whether you can argue that only a small, complete set of local configurations can cause a self-touch, so no segment is ever compared against all earlier ones.

Erect the Fence.tests: Building the boundary of a point set by walking sorted points and undoing any turn that bends the wrong way, then deciding what collinear points deserve.

Nth Magical Number.tests: Whether you can count how many qualifying numbers lie at or below a guess, then search over that monotone count instead of enumerating multiples one by one.

Add Strings.tests: Whether you can perform schoolbook addition from the least significant end without ever parsing to a native integer, including the carry that outlives the loop.

Perfect Squares.tests: Recognizing fewest-terms-summing-to-n as a coin-change shape whose denominations happen to be squares, rather than a search over combinations of them.

Palindrome Number.tests: Whether you can mirror-test a number arithmetically, choosing how much of it to rebuild so the reconstruction cannot overflow a type the input itself fits in.

Fibonacci Number.tests: Whether you can turn a two-term recurrence into a pair of rolling variables, so nothing is recomputed and nothing is stored beyond the last two values.

Integer to English Words.tests: Whether you can carve a number into repeating three-digit groups and name each identically, keeping irregular teens and empty groups from corrupting the spacing.

Add Two Numbers.tests: Whether you can carry across two lists of unequal length in a single pass, treating the exhausted list as zeros and the leftover carry as one more node.

Plus One.tests: Whether you can reason about how far a carry can propagate, and recognize the single family of inputs that forces the result to be longer than the input.

Confusing Number.tests: Whether you can separate digits that survive a 180-degree rotation from those that do not, and account for that rotation also reversing their order.

Nim Game.tests: Recognizing that a game with a fixed small move set has losing positions in a repeating cycle, so the winner is decided by a remainder rather than a search.

Bulb Switcher.tests: Whether you can count how many toggles a position receives without performing any, noticing that divisors normally pair up and asking which positions break the pairing.

Water and Jug Problem.tests: Recognizing that pouring back and forth can only ever reach multiples of a shared divisor, which replaces a state-space search with a divisibility check.

Poor Pigs.tests: Whether you can treat each subject as a digit of information and ask how many outcomes a schedule can distinguish, instead of designing a concrete strategy first.

Add to Array-Form of Integer.tests: Whether you can fold an ordinary integer into the carry of a digit-array addition, letting one loop absorb both operands even when their lengths differ wildly.

Greatest Common Divisor of Strings.tests: Recognizing that a repeated-block relationship between two strings mirrors divisibility between their lengths, plus one cheap test that a shared block exists at all.

Count Substrings with Only One Distinct.tests: Whether you can count run by run using a closed form for how many substrings a run of equal characters contains, instead of enumerating those substrings.

Equal Rational Numbers.tests: Whether you can convert a notation containing a repeating part into an exact value, and accept that two visibly different notations can denote the same number.

Adding Two Negabinary Numbers.tests: Whether the carry rule you already know survives a negative base, where an overflowing digit propagates differently and a borrow can travel in the opposite direction.

Power of Three.tests: Whether you can test membership in a geometric sequence when the base offers no bit-level shortcut, and what a fixed integer range lets you exploit instead.

Base 7.tests: Whether you can convert between bases with repeated division and remainders, and handle the sign and the zero case that the loop itself never produces.

Sum of k-Mirror Numbers.tests: Whether you can generate candidates that already satisfy one constraint by construction rather than filtering every integer, then test the second constraint on that thin stream.

Sum of Squares of Special Elements.tests: Whether you can translate an index-divisibility condition into a single pass, keeping the statement's one-based indexing from drifting against a zero-based array.

Add Digits.tests: Whether you can find what stays invariant as digits are repeatedly summed, turning an iterative collapse into a remainder with one awkward boundary case.

Count Primes.tests: Whether you can eliminate composites in bulk by marking multiples rather than testing each number for divisibility, and where that marking loop can safely start.

Pow(x, n).tests: Whether you can halve the exponent instead of decrementing it, and handle a negative exponent whose magnitude may not be representable once simply negated.
